issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

vignette:
Arthur, a 52-year-old film director, had always thrived in the chaotic energy of a film set. That changed eighteen months ago during a night shoot for a dramatic thriller. He was in the dark, overseeing a complex crane operation when a critical rigging component catastrophically failed. The deafening crash of falling equipment, followed by a blinding flash of sparks and the screams of injured crew, etched itself into his mind. Though physically unharmed, Arthur found himself trapped in a new reality.

In the aftermath, his mind replayed the incident with terrifying clarity. His memories of the frightening event were mostly pictures or images – the collapsing metal, the desperate faces, the sudden darkness – vivid and detailed, yet he couldn't seem to put the experience into words. It felt like a reel constantly looping, but without a script. These persistent, nonverbal recollections began to erode his sense of self. He found himself increasingly convinced that he was inadequate, a "bad coper" whose reactions since the event showed he was simply lousy at handling crisis. The person he had become felt utterly unrecognisable to him, a hollowed-out version of his former self. This belief that he was a 'bad coper' directly fuelled his attempts to distract himself or endlessly ponder the 'why' of the event, as he desperately sought to understand his perceived failings.

What frightened Arthur most was the constant, gnawing sense of danger. This pervasive sense of danger was deeply intertwined with his negative self-appraisals, as his conviction of being an inadequate 'coper' intensified his belief that he was inherently vulnerable and the world remained perilous. The vivid, visual memories of the accident kept him on edge, making him hypervigilant, superalert and watchful. Any unexpected or loud sounds now sent a jolt through him, leaving him on high alert, scanning his surroundings. He found himself jumping or startling at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people – the sudden clatter of a prop on set, a car backfiring outside his editing suite, even the doorbell at home. This constant state of heightened threat became unbearable, and in response, Arthur began to avoid circumstances that reminded him of the event. He started turning down night shoots, refusing to work in enclosed, dark spaces, and even found himself steering clear of sets with complex rigging. He also found himself trying to distract himself with something else whenever the memories surfaced, or pondering why the event had happened to him, though these thoughts rarely brought comfort or clarity. Ironically, these very attempts to suppress or intellectualise the event seemed to paradoxically keep the vivid, nonverbal memories looping, preventing their natural processing.

His avoidance, however, only tightened the loop of his suffering. Because he was constantly on guard and startling at sounds, he increasingly avoided any situation that might trigger these reactions, including his own film sets. This withdrawal, in turn, reinforced his negative self-perceptions; every cancelled meeting or declined project was further proof that he was indeed a lousy coper and inadequate, deepening the belief that the person he had become was unrecognisable. His partner, Maria, noticed his increasing isolation, the way he would suddenly freeze at a car horn, or how he insisted on leaving every light on in their apartment after dusk. By avoiding the very environments where he might confront his fears and gradually disconfirm the perceived threat, Arthur inadvertently maintained his hypervigilance. The less he exposed himself to the realities of a working set, the more dangerous it felt in his mind, and the more these avoidance behaviours confirmed his belief that he was fundamentally broken.

Arthur had come to a point where his career, his relationship, and his very identity felt hostage to the accident. He finally sought help, hoping to reclaim some semblance of the director he once was, terrified that he might never escape the tightening grip of his own mind.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not explicitly state that Arthur's negative self-appraisals directly cause or lead to his maladaptive coping strategies.
The vignette does not establish a causal link where Arthur's negative self-appraisals directly contribute to his sense of threat or hypervigilance.
The vignette describes maladaptive strategies as responses to memories or threat, but not as a cause or influence on the presence or nature of the intrusive memories themselves.
